GCD × LCM = M × N

Number TheoryArithmeticInvariants
Game: See how tiling a rectangle with equal squares explains a surprising link between the gcd and lcm of two numbers.
How to play: Change M and N with the number boxes and watch the three rectangles update.
Look for the math

Two numbers multiplied together equal their greatest common divisor times their least common multiple. A picture of tiled rectangles shows why.

The largest square that tiles

The greatest common divisor G = gcd(M, N) is exactly the side of the largest square that tiles an M by N rectangle. It takes S = (M/G)(N/G) such squares. Splitting each G by G square into G strips gives S·G small rectangles — and that number is divisible by both M and N.

The least common multiple

The two extra rectangles show S·G as (M/G)·N strips and as M·(N/G) strips. This common multiple is the least possible: a larger common strip would mean a larger square also tiles the original rectangle, contradicting the maximality of G. Hence S·G is the least common multiple, and M·N = gcd·lcm.

Why min + max wins

For each prime, the exponent in the gcd is the smaller of the two exponents and in the lcm the larger. Since min + max = a + b, the exponents on both sides match. The logic test checks the identity and all three rectangle counts for every pair M, N from 1 to 40 — 1,600 cases — and confirms the gcd against Euclid's algorithm.

Try M = 12 and N = 10. How many G by G squares fill the first rectangle, and what is the lcm?
